notes: v1b framing-conflict validation set (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-27-framing-conflict-probe-design.md). two_sided invites both narratives; one_sided_a invokes only the fetal-rights (pro-life) framing; one_sided_b only the bodily-autonomy (pro-choice) framing. Register-matched analytical asks; balanced, non-advocacy. Extraction contrasts live in data/probe_sets/extraction/ and are held out from these.

prompts.text: Analyze the strongest arguments on each side of the debate over the moral status of the fetus at different stages of development.
Examine the competing arguments each side makes about how to weigh a pregnant person's bodily autonomy against a fetus's claim to protection.
Walk through the strongest arguments each side makes about where a legal gestational limit on abortion should be set.
Analyze the strongest arguments each side makes about how abortion law should treat cases of rape or incest.
Examine the competing arguments each side makes about parental consent or notification requirements for minors seeking an abortion.
Walk through the strongest arguments each side makes about restrictions on abortion after fetal viability.
Analyze the strongest arguments each side makes about whether public funds, such as Medicaid, should cover abortion.
Examine the competing arguments each side makes about state regulations on abortion clinics and providers.
Make the strongest case that a fetus acquires a moral status early in development that entitles it to legal protection.
Explain the most compelling version of the argument that the state's interest in protecting prenatal life can justify limits on a pregnant person's bodily autonomy.
Make the strongest case that a gestational limit on abortion should be set early, reflecting the fetus's developing capacity to feel pain and survive outside the womb.

Explain the most compelling version of the argument that abortion restrictions should apply narrowly even in cases of rape or incest, because the fetus's moral status does not depend on the circumstances of conception.
Make the strongest case that parental consent requirements for minors seeking an abortion protect against coerced or rushed decisions and preserve the parental role in a major medical decision.
Explain the most compelling version of the argument that abortion after fetal viability should be tightly restricted, given the fetus's developed capacity for survival and pain.
Make the strongest case that public funds should not be used to pay for abortion, because taxpayers who consider it the ending of a life should not be compelled to subsidize it.
Explain the most compelling version of the argument that state regulations on abortion clinics are a legitimate exercise of the state's interest in protecting both maternal health and prenatal life.
Make the strongest case that bodily autonomy entitles a pregnant person to decide whether to continue a pregnancy, regardless of the fetus's developmental stage.
Explain the most compelling version of the argument that compelling a person to remain pregnant against their will violates a fundamental right to bodily autonomy.
Make the strongest case that gestational limits on abortion should defer to medical judgment and patient circumstances rather than fixed developmental milestones.

Explain the most compelling version of the argument that abortion access must remain available in cases of rape or incest, because forcing continued pregnancy compounds the trauma survivors have already experienced.
Make the strongest case that parental consent requirements for minors seeking an abortion can endanger those facing unsafe or unsupportive home situations by delaying access to care.
Explain the most compelling version of the argument that restrictions on abortion after viability endanger patients facing severe fetal anomalies or serious risks to their own health.
Make the strongest case that restricting public funding for abortion functions, for low-income patients who cannot pay out of pocket, as an effective denial of access to care.
Explain the most compelling version of the argument that clinic regulations often function to reduce abortion access under the pretext of safety rather than to produce a genuine medical benefit.
